question: What does the Most-Favoured-Nation (MFN) principle require under the GATT?
reference_answer: Any advantage, favour, privilege or immunity granted by a contracting party to any product originating in or destined for any other country must be accorded immediately and unconditionally to the like product originating in or destined for the territories of all other contracting parties.
answer:
Under the GATT, the Most-Favoured-Nation (MFN) principle requires that:

> "...any advantage, favour, privilege or immunity granted by any contracting party to any product originating in or destined for any other country shall be accorded immediately and unconditionally to the like product originating in or destined for the territories of all other contracting parties" [GATT Art. I].

This requirement applies to:
* Customs duties and charges of any kind imposed on or in connection with importation or exportation, or imposed on the international transfer of payments for imports or exports [GATT Art. I];
* The method of levying such duties and charges [GATT Art. I];
* All rules and formalities in connection with importation and exportation [GATT Art. I]; and
* All matters referred to in paragraphs 2 and 4 of Article III [GATT Art. I].

question: Can a country impose higher internal sales taxes on imported goods than on like domestic products?
reference_answer: No. Imported products shall not be subject, directly or indirectly, to internal taxes or other internal charges in excess of those applied to like domestic products.
answer:
**No**, a country cannot impose internal taxes on imported goods "in excess of those applied, directly or indirectly, to like domestic products" [GATT Art. III:2].

Under GATT 1994, imported products:
> shall not be subject, directly or indirectly, to internal taxes or other internal charges of any kind in excess of those applied, directly or indirectly, to like domestic products [GATT Art. III:2].

Furthermore, internal taxes must not be applied to imported or domestic products "so as to afford protection to domestic production" [GATT Art. III:1].

question: What is the general rule on quantitative restrictions like import quotas under the GATT?
reference_answer: They are generally prohibited: no prohibitions or restrictions other than duties, taxes or other charges, whether made effective through quotas, import or export licences or other measures, may be instituted or maintained on imports or exports.
answer:
Under the GATT, the general rule is a strict prohibition on quantitative restrictions. 

Specifically, Article XI:1 provides:
> "No prohibitions or restrictions other than duties, taxes or other charges, whether made effective through quotas, import or export licences or other measures, shall be instituted or maintained by any contracting party on the importation of any product of the territory of any other contracting party or on the exportation or sale for export of any product destined for the territory of any other contracting party [GATT Art. question: Under what condition can a Member levy an anti-dumping duty under the GATT?
reference_answer: Only if the effect of the dumping is to cause or threaten material injury to an established domestic industry, or to materially retard the establishment of a domestic industry (VI:6(a)); the duty may not be greater than the margin of dumping (VI:2).
answer:
Under the GATT, a Member may levy an anti-dumping duty on a dumped product only if it determines that the effect of the dumping:

* is such as to **"cause or threaten material injury to an established domestic industry, or is such as to retard materially the establishment of a domestic industry"** [GATT Art. VI:6(a)].

Additionally, the anti-dumping duty levied must be **"not greater in amount than the margin of dumping in respect of such product"** [GATT Art. VI:2]. 

Dumping itself is considered to occur when products of one country are introduced into the commerce of another country at **"less than the normal value of the products"** [GATT Art. VI:1].

question: What criteria must an invention meet to be patentable under TRIPS?
reference_answer: It must be new, involve an inventive step and be capable of industrial application; patents must be available in all fields of technology, subject to paragraphs 2 and 3.
answer:
Under TRIPS, patents must be available for **"any inventions, whether products or processes, in all fields of technology, provided that they are new, involve an inventive step and are capable of industrial application"** [TRIPS Art. 27:1]. 

The agreement also specifies the following regarding these criteria:
* **Synonyms for terms:** Members may deem the terms "inventive step" and "capable of industrial application" to be synonymous with "non-obvious" and "useful", respectively [TRIPS Art. 27:1 fn 5].
* **Non-discrimination:** Patents must be available and patent rights enjoyable without discrimination as to the place of invention, the field of technology, and whether products are imported or locally produced [TRIPS Art. 27:1].
* **Disclosure condition:** Applicants must "disclose the invention in a manner sufficiently clear and complete for the invention to be carried out by a person skilled in the art" and may be required to indicate the best mode for carrying it out [TRIPS Art. 29:1].

Members may exclude certain subject matter from patentability, such as inventions necessary to protect *ordre public* or morality (including human, animal, or plant life/health, or to avoid serious prejudice to the environment), diagnostic, therapeutic, and surgical methods for treatment, and certain plants, animals, and essentially biological processes [TRIPS Art. 27:2-3].

question: Does the DSU allow a Member to unilaterally determine that another Member has violated a WTO agreement and retaliate on its own?
reference_answer: No. Members must have recourse to and abide by the DSU; they may not make their own determination that a violation has occurred except through dispute settlement under the DSU, and must obtain DSB authorization before suspending concessions.

When Members seek the redress of a violation or nullification/impairment of benefits, they must have recourse to, and abide by, the rules and procedures of the DSU [DSU Art. 23:1]. Specifically, Members shall:

* **Not make unilateral determinations:** Members shall "not make a determination to the effect that a violation has occurred, that benefits have been nullified or impaired or that the attainment of any objective of the covered agreements has been impeded, except through recourse to dispute settlement in accordance with the rules and procedures of this Understanding, and shall make any such determination consistent with the findings contained in the panel or Appellate Body report adopted by the DSB or an arbitration award rendered under this Understanding" [DSU Art. 23:2(a)].
* **Obtain authorization before retaliating:** Members must follow the prescribed procedures to determine the reasonable period of time for implementation [DSU Art. 23:2(b)], and must "obtain DSB authorization in accordance with those procedures before suspending concessions or other obligations under the covered agreements in response to the failure of maxSum Member concerned to implement the recommendations and rulings within that reasonable period of time" [DSU Art. 23:2(c)].

question: How does the scope of National Treatment differ between the GATT and the GATS?
reference_answer: Under GATT Article III national treatment applies to all imported products. Under GATS Article XVII it applies only in the sectors inscribed in a Member's Schedule and subject to the conditions and qualifications set out there.

The scope of National Treatment differs significantly between the GATT and the GATS in terms of their application as general obligations versus specific commitments, as well as their substantive reach:

* **General Obligation vs. Specific Commitment:** Under the GATT, National Treatment is a **general obligation** that applies broadly to internal taxes, regulations, and requirements affecting products once they are imported [GATT Art. III:1-III:4]. By contrast, under the GATS, National Treatment is a **specific commitment** that applies only "In the sectors inscribed in its Schedule, and subject to any conditions and qualifications set out therein" [GATS Art. XVII:1].
* **Subject Matter:** The GATT applies to imported "products" in respect of internal taxes, internal charges, laws, regulations, and requirements affecting their internal sale, offering for sale, purchase, transportation, distribution, or use [GATT Art. III:1-III:4]. The GATS applies to "services and service suppliers of any other Member, in respect of all measures affecting the supply of services" across the four modes of supply defined in the agreement [GATS Art. XVII:1, GATS Art. I:2].
* **Form of Treatment:** The GATS explicitly clarifies that National Treatment may be met through "either formally identical treatment or formally different treatment," and specifies that "[f]ormally identical or formally different treatment shall be considered to be less favourable if it modifies the conditions of competition in favour of services or service suppliers of the Member compared to like services or service suppliers of any other Member" [GATS Art. XVII:2-XVII:3].

question: How do the security exceptions in GATT and GATS compare regarding essential security interests?
reference_answer: Both say nothing requires a Member to disclose information contrary to its essential security interests or prevents action it considers necessary to protect them (e.g. fissionable materials, military supply, war or other emergency in international relations), or action under the UN Charter. GATS XIV bis:2 adds that the Council for Trade in Services must be informed to the fullest extent possible of such measures and their termination.
answer:
The security exceptions in GATT (Article XXI) and GATS (Article XIV bis) are structurally and textually nearly identical, but differ in their substantive scope (goods versus services) and in one procedural requirement present in GATS.

### Similarities
Both provisions protect a Member’s prerogative regarding "essential security interests" by allowing a Member:
* **To withhold information:** Not "to require any [contracting party / Member] to furnish any information the disclosure of which it considers contrary to its essential security interests" [GATT Art. XXI(a), GATS Art. XIV bis 1(a)].
* **To take necessary action:** Not to prevent taking "any action which it considers necessary for the protection of its essential security interests" [GATT Art. XXI(b), GATS Art. XIV bis 1(b)].
* **To address specific domains:** Both explicitly cover actions:
  * "relating to fissionable materials or the materials from which they are derived" (GATS also explicitly adds "fusionable" materials) [GATT Art. XXI(b)(i), GATS Art. XIV bis 1(b)(ii)].
  * "taken in time of war or other emergency in international relations" [GATT Art. XXI(b)(iii), GATS Art. XIV bis 1(b)(iii)].
* **To uphold UN obligations:** Both allow actions taken "in pursuance of its obligations under the United Nations Charter for the maintenance of international peace and security" [GATT Art. XXI(c), GATS Art. XIV bis 1(c)].

### Differences
1. **Scope of Application (Goods vs. Services):** 
   * **GATT Article XXI(b)(ii)** covers actions "relating to the traffic in arms, ammunition and implements of war and to such traffic in other goods and materials as is carried on directly or indirectly for the purpose of supplying a military establishment" [GATT Art. XXI(b)(ii)].
   * **GATS Article XIV bis 1(b)(i)** instead covers actions "relating to the supply of services as carried out directly or indirectly for the purpose of provisioning a military establishment" [GATS Art. XIV bis 1(b)(i)].
2. **Procedural Requirement:** 
   * **GATS Article XIV bis (paragraph 2)** contains an explicit reporting obligation: "The Council for Trade in Services shall be informed to the fullest extent possible of measures taken under paragraphs 1(b) and (c) and of their termination" [GATS Art. XIV bis]. 
   * **GATT Article XXI** contains no corresponding explicit requirement to inform a council of measures taken.

question: Under TRIPS, can a Member override a patent through a compulsory license, and if so, what is the standard requirement regarding prior negotiation with the right holder?
reference_answer: Yes. Article 28 grants the patent owner exclusive rights, but Article 31 allows other use without authorization if its conditions are met; under 31(b) the proposed user must first have tried to obtain authorization on reasonable commercial terms within a reasonable period, a requirement that can be waived for a national emergency, other extreme urgency or public non-commercial use.

Yes, a Member may allow for the use of the subject matter of a patent without the authorization of the right holder (a compulsory license or "other use without authorization of the right holder") [TRIPS Art. 31(a)-(f)]. 

Regarding the standard requirement for prior negotiation with the right holder:
* **General Rule:** Such use may only be permitted if, "prior to such use, the proposed user has made efforts to obtain authorization from the right holder on reasonable commercial terms and conditions and that such efforts have not been successful within a reasonable period of time" [TRIPS Art. 31(b)].
* **Waiver:** "This requirement may be waived by a Member in the case of a national emergency or other circumstances of extreme urgency or in cases of public non-commercial use" [TRIPS Art. 31(b)]. 
* **Post-grant notification:** In situations of national emergency or extreme urgency, the right holder must "nevertheless, be notified as soon as reasonably practicable" [TRIPS Art. 31(b)]. In cases of public non-commercial use, where the government or contractor knows or has demonstrable grounds to know that a valid patent is or will be used without making a patent search, the right holder must "be informed promptly" [TRIPS Art. 31(b)].
* **Anti-competitive practices:** Members are also "not obliged to apply the conditions set forth in subparagraphs (b) and (f) where such use is permitted to remedy a practice determined after judicial or administrative process to be anti-competitive" [TRIPS Art. 31(k)].

question: If a Member fails to comply with a WTO panel ruling, what are the two temporary remedies available under the DSU and in what order should concessions be suspended?
reference_answer: Compensation (voluntary) and DSB-authorized suspension of concessions or other obligations. Under Article 22.3 the complaining party should first suspend in the same sector, then in other sectors under the same agreement, and only then under another covered agreement.
answer:
The two temporary measures available are **compensation** and **the suspension of concessions or other obligations** [DSU Art. 22.1]. 

Neither compensation nor the suspension of concessions is preferred to full implementation of a recommendation to bring a measure into conformity, and compensation is voluntary [DSU Art. 22.1]. Both are temporary measures available if recommendations and rulings are not implemented within a reasonable period of time [DSU Art. 22.1].

Regarding the order in which concessions or other obligations should be suspended, the complaining party must follow these principles and procedures:

question: How do GATT and GATS handle regional trade agreements like free-trade areas or economic integration agreements?
reference_answer: GATT Article XXIV permits customs unions and free-trade areas that eliminate duties and other restrictive regulations on substantially all the trade between the parties, without raising barriers to other Members. GATS Article V permits agreements that have substantial sectoral coverage and eliminate substantially all discrimination, without raising the overall level of barriers to non-parties.
answer:
GATT and GATS handle regional trade agreements (such as customs unions, free-trade areas, and economic integration agreements) by permitting their formation as exceptions to the general obligation of most-favoured-nation (MFN) treatment, provided that the agreements meet specific structural, coverage, and transparency requirements designed to facilitate trade without raising external barriers.

### 1. GATT 1994 (Goods)
Under **GATT Article XXIV**, the provisions of the Agreement do not prevent the formation of a customs union or a free-trade area, or an interim agreement necessary to form them, subject to the following core conditions:
* **Purpose:** The purpose of a customs union or free-trade area "should be to facilitate trade between the constituent territories and not to raise barriers to the trade of other contracting parties with such territories" [GATT Art. XXIV:4].
* **Elimination of Barriers:** For a **free-trade area**, "duties and other restrictive regulations of commerce (except, where necessary, those permitted under Articles XI, XII, XIII, XIV, XV and XX) are eliminated on substantially all the trade between the constituent territories in products originating in such territories" [GATT Art. XXIV:8(b)]. For a **customs union**, similar elimination applies to substantially all trade within the union, and substantially the same duties and regulations are applied to non-members [GATT Art. XXIV:8(a)].
* **External Trade Barriers:** The duties and other regulations of commerce imposed at the formation of any customs union or interim agreement in respect of trade with non-parties "shall not on balance be higher or more restrictive than the general incidence of the duties and regulations of commerce applicable in the constituent territories prior to the formation of such union" [GATT Art. XXIV:5(a)].
* **Notification and Review:** Any contracting party entering into a customs union, free-trade area, or interim agreement must "promptly notify the CONTRACTING PARTIES and shall make available to them such information regarding the proposed union or area as will enable them to make such reports and recommendations" [GATT Art. XXIV:7(a)].

### 2. GATS (Services)
Under **GATS Article V**, Members are not prevented from being a party to or entering into an agreement liberalizing trade in services, provided the agreement meets specific integration criteria:
* **Substantial Coverage:** The agreement must have "substantial sectoral coverage" (understood in terms of number of sectors, volume of trade affected, and modes of supply, without a priori exclusion of any mode of supply) [GATS Art. V:1(a) & fn 1].
* **Absence or Elimination of Discrimination:** The agreement must provide for "the absence or elimination of substantially all discrimination, in the sense of Article XVII, between or among the parties, in the sectors covered... either at the entry into force of that agreement or on the basis of a reasonable time-frame" [GATS Art. V:1(b)].
* **External Barriers:** Any such agreement "shall be designed to facilitate trade between the parties to the agreement and shall not in respect of any Member outside the agreement raise the overall level of barriers to trade in services within the respective sectors or subsectors compared to the level applicable prior to such an agreement" [GATS Art. V:4].
* **Flexibility for Developing Countries:** When developing countries are parties to such agreements, "flexibility shall be provided for regarding the conditions set out in paragraph 1... in accordance with the level of development of the countries concerned" [GATS Art. V:3(a)].
* **Notification:** Agreements must be promptly notified to the Council for Trade in Services, which may establish working parties to examine their consistency with Article V [GATS Art. V:7(a)]. Additionally, GATS Article V bis allows for agreements establishing full integration of labor markets under specific conditions [GATS Art. V bis].

question: Are there any restrictions on the general security exception?
reference_answer: Yes, in the text: the exception covers only information the Member considers contrary to its essential security interests, action it considers necessary for those interests in the listed situations (fissionable materials; arms, ammunition and military supply; war or other emergency in international relations), and action under the UN Charter for international peace and security. GATS XIV bis also requires informing the Council for Trade in Services. How far 'which it considers' can be reviewed is not addressed in the corpus.
answer:
Under GATT 1994, GATS, and TRIPS, the security exceptions (which apply when a Member takes action **"which it considers necessary for the protection of its essential security interests"**) are conditioned by specific circumstances [GATT Art. XXI, GATS Art. XIV bis, TRIPS Art. 73]. 

Specifically, the action must be one:
* **(i)** relating to fissionable materials or the materials from which they are derived [GATT Art. XXI(b)(i), GATS Art. XIV bis(1)(b)(ii), TRIPS Art. 73(b)(i)];
* **(ii)** relating to the traffic in arms, ammunition and implements of war and to such traffic in other goods and materials as is carried on directly or indirectly for the purpose of supplying a military establishment (or, under GATS, relating to the supply of services carried out directly or indirectly for the purpose of provisioning a military establishment) [GATT Art. XXI(b)(ii), GATS Art. XIV bis(1)(b)(i), TRIPS Art. 73(b)(ii)];
* **(iii)** taken in time of war or other emergency in international relations [GATT Art. XXI(b)(iii), GATS Art. XIV bis(1)(b)(iii), TRIPS Art. 73(b)(iii)]; or
* **(iv)** taken in pursuance of a Member's obligations under the United Nations Charter for the maintenance of international peace and security [GATT Art. XXI(c), GATS Art. XIV bis(1)(c), TRIPS Art. 73(c)].

Additionally, under GATS, **"The Council for Trade in Services shall be informed to the fullest extent possible of measures taken under paragraphs 1(b) and (c) and of their termination."** [GATS Art. XIV bis(2)].

question: Can a country tax its own domestic products more heavily than the same product imported from a foreign country?
reference_answer: The text does not prohibit it: Article III:2 only protects imported products from internal taxes in excess of those applied to like domestic products; it says nothing against taxing domestic products more.

question: What exception is applicable to restricting the entrance of potentially toxic plants into a country?
reference_answer: GATT Article XX(b) (measures necessary to protect human, animal or plant life or health), with the SPS Agreement governing such measures: Article 2.1 gives Members the right to take SPS measures, and Annex A para. 1 covers risks from the entry of pests (which include weeds) and toxins; measures must be science-based and no more trade-restrictive than necessary.
answer:
Under GATT 1994, the general exception applicable to restricting the entrance of potentially toxic plants is **GATT Article XX(b)**, which permits measures:

> "necessary to protect human, animal or plant life or health" [GATT Art. XX(a)-(i)].

To be justified under Article XX, such measures must also satisfy the requirements of the Article's introductory clause (chapeau), meaning they must not be applied in a manner that would constitute:
> "a means of arbitrary or unjustifiable discrimination between countries where the same conditions prevail, or a disguised restriction on international trade" [GATT Art. XX(a)-(i)].

Additionally, under the **Agreement on the Application of Sanitary and Phytosanitary Measures (SPS Agreement)**, Members have the right to take phytosanitary measures:
> "necessary for the protection of human, animal or plant life or health, provided that such measures are not inconsistent with the provisions of this Agreement" [SPS Art. 2:1].

Such SPS measures must be applied only to the extent necessary, be based on scientific principles, and not be maintained without sufficient scientific evidence [SPS Art. 2:2]. Measures conforming to the SPS Agreement are presumed to be in accordance with GATT 1994, in particular Article XX(b) [SPS Art. 2:4].

question: Can intellectual property rights ever be suspended?
reference_answer: Yes, in two senses in the corpus: under DSU Article 22.3(f)(iii) a complaining party authorized by the DSB may suspend obligations under the TRIPS Agreement as retaliation; and TRIPS Article 31 allows use of a patent without the right holder's authorization (compulsory licensing) under strict conditions.
answer:
Yes, the TRIPS Agreement allows for the "use of the subject matter of a patent without the authorization of the right holder, including use by the government or third parties authorized by the government" (often referred to as compulsory licensing) [TRIPS Art. 31]. 

When such use is permitted, it is subject to strict conditions, including:
* **Authorization on individual merits:** "authorization of such use shall be considered on its individual merits" [TRIPS Art. 31(a)].
* **Prior negotiation:** Generally, the user must make prior efforts to obtain authorization from the right holder on reasonable commercial terms, though this requirement "may be waived by a Member in the case of a national emergency or other circumstances of extreme urgency or in cases of public non-commercial use" [TRIPS Art. 31(b)].
* **Scope and duration:** "the scope and duration of such use shall be limited to the purpose for which it was authorized" [TRIPS Art. 31(c)].
* **Remuneration:** "the right holder shall be paid adequate remuneration in the circumstances of each case, taking into account the economic value of the authorization" [TRIPS Art. 31(h)].
* **Termination:** Authorization is "liable, subject to adequate protection of the legitimate interests of the persons so authorized, to be terminated if and when the circumstances which led to it cease to exist and are unlikely to recur" [TRIPS Art. 31(g)].

Additionally, patents can be subject to revocation or forfeiture, provided that "[a]n opportunity for judicial review of any decision to revoke or forfeit a patent shall be available" [TRIPS Art. 32]. Members may also adopt measures to control abuse of intellectual property rights in licensing practices that adversely affect competition [TRIPS Art. 40].
